speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This interview with Palma Hanson Hove was recorded at her home in Moscow on June 13th, 1975. The interviewer is Sam Schrager. What happened to Genesee Valley?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: I don't know exactly, only that he was on his own and wanted to go west and sort of worked his way from Wisconsin until he got, well, like I told you before, he logged up in the Blue Mountains for a long time and drove oxen team and all that sort of stuff. I suppose he probably met somebody that was going to Genesee. Now I'm just not too sure about this, but I think that's the way it was. It seems to me like I heard him say that it was a fellow by the name of Tenis Miller that he met and he was going to Genesee. So he went along and got work and then just liked it there and stayed.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He had been born in Wisconsin?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yes, he was born in Wisconsin. I expect he was about, oh, let me see if it says anything in my scrapbook about that. It's right in there. What year he came out here? May 17, 1863. He went to Walla Walla in the spring of 1888 and in the fall of 1889 he came to Genesee. So he was logging with oxen teams for a long time, followed the same business here, arriving at the same time. Let's see. When Genesee was moving from Old Town he assisted in moving some of the building with his yokes of oxen. The Old Town was further out past the elevators at that time. So he helped move the buildings into, which is Genesee now. They were married by the Reverend Thomas Guard, which you mentioned one time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Your mother was born in Norway?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yes, she was born in, well, it's a little town in Norway. Well, at Trondheim, Norway, she was born.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever know why her parents came over to America?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Some of their people came first to America and then they'd send for them. If they were here a while and had a little bit of money, then they'd send for some of the rest of them and then they'd have to work their passage out after they got here. It would take quite a few years sometimes if you had a family. But that's, they came to Sioux Falls, South Dakota. And it just goes on from there telling.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did her father have to work his passage, do you know?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh, I'm sure he did. Yeah, yes, in fact I know he did. But I can't remember, it must have just been a cousin or somebody that came first of his, of my mother's father. And then they took up a homestead and then they worked for them until. But I know they lived in a sod house because they didn't have buildings, you know. So they lived in a sod house for quite a few years. And then first my uncle came out west and then he sent for his parents and then my mother came and so that's the way they did, you know. They just sent for, until they got all the family out. And they seemed to, you know, manage some way. I don't know how they did it, but they did.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think Genesee was a very attractive place for people to come and set up?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: There was so much good farmland here, you see. And that was the reason that, and the soil was very good. And at that time, because my folks didn't take a homestead, that was before they came that they had homestead rights. But some of the people did that came. I bet you Mr. Hagen could tell you about that. But by the time my folks came or were ready to buy land, there was no more homesteads to get. You'd have to go to the timber for that above Troy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Isn't that what they did? Didn't you tell me who had the homestead?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: My grandmother, my mother's parents had the homestead up above Troy. And they lived there until they proved up on their, like they say, proved up on their homestead. But while they were there, they made shingles and cut wood, you know, and made their living that way, selling cordwood and shingles. I can remember the shingle camp real good. They'd just get a little hole in the timber, you know, and then put sort of a roof over so you wouldn't get wet if it was raining. And they sat under that and made those shingles by hand. I can remember that real well. They decided to live near Troy because they could get a homestead. Yes, uh-huh, that was it. And my uncle only had 40 acres, but after they had proven up on their homestead, and they were getting quite old by that time, then they came back to Genesee Valley and lived on my uncle's 40. And then they lived there until they weren't able to live alone, then they lived with my folks.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think it would have been hard for them as older people to homestead?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, it was hard, but they did it. They had a team of horses, you know, and they, you bet it was hard. Had a few cows, you know, so they got their butter and cream and made shingles and stuff enough to buy some flour and sugar and, you know, the other. There was no luxuries, let me tell you that. Made their own cheese. I can see those cheese forms yet. I wish to goodness, you know, that I'd kept some of that stuff. But, you know, when we were growing up and that stuff was around, well that was junk. I give my eye teeth for some of those things now. But you just never even thought about that someday they would be valuable. I managed to keep my grandmother's spinning wheel, for which I'm very thankful. You remember going up there from the trips to the...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah, that would be about, oh goodness, how far would it be crossroad from Genesee, well we were four miles north of Genesee. Well, it would be about twelve miles to Moscow and then twelve miles... No, we didn't go to Moscow. That's right, you came... We went crossroad. But I daresay up to where my grandfather was, it must have been twenty miles at least. And we used to go off and ride up there in the lumber wagon. My father would bring wood back, you know. So I... yeah, that was a great trip to get to go up to the timber. What was the trip like? Was it an exhausting trip for a kid?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, you know, in those days it wasn't. I suppose we got tired, but we were kids and we had a lot of cousins up there to play with, you know, when we got there. Because my uncle, that is my real aunt and her husband, they had a homestead right next to my grandmother and grandfather. So they weren't up there alone. And then a neighbor of ours, they also had a homestead there. And they lived there until the kids were big enough to go to school. There was no school up there, of course. They had to go down to Troy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Can you remember what the country looked like on the drive? Was it all settled up by then?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, oh no, no. No going from Troy out to the timber where they lived. It was just narrow dirt road, you know, and rough and very few houses. I suppose there were homesteads.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So I don't know what a homestead consisted of.

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: 80 or 60 acres? Something like that, I suppose. Up to 160. Probably. And you would meet, you know, go by a few places, but not very many. It was kind of wild and secluded.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would you kids play at?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh my, well, I don't know, of course, to us, just walking down the lanes in the timber and picking flowers and watching them make shakes and all that was just a thrill, you know, because we had never lived up there in the timber. I remember my grandmother, they had a log cabin and there was no ceiling, you know, it was just rafters. And I remember that I slept on a cot and I looked up and there was a rat sitting up on one of the rafters. And oh, I was so scared, of course. And grandma said, oh, that won't hurt you, she said. They're just pets. So it was really kind of fun. Couldn't thought of it for a long, long time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you feel the big difference between that being timber country as compared to Genesee and farmland?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yes, oh yes, definitely. Because, you know, down there we had our wide open spaces and up there it was just really thick with trees. It wasn't the best timber in the world, but then it was timber that they could make fence posts and shakes and shingles and stuff like that out of.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they plant at all? Did they have a crop?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, I think a little bit wild, or a little bit oats in places where it was cleared off. Just enough for hay in the winter time. Other than that, it was mostly pasture, you know, in the summer knoll. It was, I don't remember ever raising any wheat or anything like that up there because the ground wasn't cleared that much. It was just, like I say, just timber.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there a very close relationship between the Norwegian community at Genesee and the one near Troy?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, no. No, we hardly, we didn't know anybody hardly in Troy. I guess the folks knew one or two families there that they had met. But no, it was too far to commute between for visiting or anything like that. Unless you were relatives. Yeah, but in the later years we had relatives living in Troy, but at the time that my grandparents lived, that's as far as we went. It was up to their place, not to our uncle's place.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where was their place from, Troy?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, it would be north. It's kind of like above Spring Valley up in there. Further north, I think, than Spring Valley. That's still right in the timbered country. Oh yes, uh-huh. I wonder if their place is being farmed now or if it's gone back to Tim. No, I don't believe it's ever been cleared for farming that I know of. I think it's just sort of, you know how some of that soil was. It was very light. And then another thing, it's always so late that crops would freeze. But as I remember it was just a little oat that my families raised up there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what was your home like where you grew up on your Genesee?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh, well, the house is still there. Although, do you remember here a little while back where there was an airplane went down? Right, that's where I was born and raised. And those fir trees that were in the back my father brought down from my grandmother's place up there in the timber and planted them. There was a whole row of them for a windbreak. That's the place. My house is still there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This is on Cow Creek?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Uh-huh, oh yes. Well, you know where Fred Hobies lived. Well, this was right over the fence from where they live now, where my home was.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it small when you were just a kid or had they already built it to its present size?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, my father added to it. He built a little home for my grandparents right by our place, right about, you know, the length of the house away from ours. And then after they passed away, he moved that little house up next to ours and made a bathroom and bedroom and stuff out of it. So, we added some to it. But my father and another man built the house in the first place. And it was only just, it was a two-story but, you know, just not very big. Although we were ten kids.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did it work? Would there be a bunch of kids in one in each bedroom?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yes, well, we had an upstairs, and I think we had three rooms upstairs, and the boys had two, three beds in one part and we girls had the other. Of course, there was only eight that lived, so. But we always had somebody staying there. My uncle practically lived at our place for years and years. And my cousin used to come there and stay in the wintertime and I don't know how they did it, but they managed somehow. Did you feel crowded when you were... Oh indeed we did. We felt crowded alright. But we had what they call a summer kitchen. And in the wintertime they'd put a bed out there too and had a little stove out there to heat it, you know. Are you taking this on tape?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove or Sam Schrager
words: Oh, crying out for it. Of course. Oh, that's really something. Well, it's much better just for it to be a conversation between us that it's much freer and tells a lot more about the past. Well, it seemed like in those days you managed somewhere or other. We didn't have very fancy food, but we had plenty.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It seems like the big... Were most of the families big?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah, they were. They were big families. Not as big as ours, all of them. But there was a lot of them had eight children in their family and seldom anybody had less than five or six. So, you know, I don't know, in our country school down there there used to be thirty, forty kids in that little one room school house. And the teacher had all eighth grades. Now, if you don't think they had something to do. But we got through. We sure did. That's as far as I got was through the eighth grade, but then I did that. By that time I was, you know, between fourteen and fifteen and I had to get out and work.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it hard for the families when you were young to get by?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yes, it was because my father only had eighty acres. And you didn't, you know, unless you had diversified farming, you know, we raised a lot of potatoes and had hogs and cows and stuff like that. But, boy, on eighty acres and try to raise a family and then probably a couple extra away, it wasn't easy. My folks lived there till, oh, I forget what year they moved into Genesee. And my father bought a mercantile store and interested in it and my brother run it. Well, first they bought a farm out of Genesee, what used to be the old town. And then they sold that and then they bought into this store. They hadn't interested in that until my father died.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They bought a farm right where old town had been?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Uh huh. They sold the farm up in the valley and bought this one downtown or down to old town. And then they bought a place right inside of city limits but it had some ground so my father had cows and milked cows and peddled milk there for a while. And then they moved from there up to the place of town where they lived until my mother died.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you were young, did he work out very much as well as the work he did on the place?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, yes, he worked out in harvest time usually but that was about all. You know, the kids were small then and he had the farming to do himself. And when the boys got big enough, well then they got out and got jobs because there wasn't enough land for them to farm. So my oldest brother went into... My father bought him a big truck and he started in with the rock business. He had rock pits and that was what he did all the time. He worked for years for Max Cuney in Spokane with rock. And then he bought his own rock pit down by Lewiston which he had until he had a real bad heart attack. Then he had to sell it. So he's gone now too. And my other brother that was in the store in Genesee, he kind of worked in stores off and on and then kind of liked that business. So then my father put him there in the store after he bought into it. My youngest brother joined the Navy and he never was here anymore. He was back east in Detroit and all over. It sounds like it wasn't so easy to be able to stay if you didn't have a farm to stay in. No, as soon as they were old enough, all of us, we sort of left and was on our own, which we had to do. But we went along fine.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you say that there was a real difference between his feeling about the men working out, the boys and his daughters working out?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah, well he never would let us girls go further away from home than Moscow. But the boys, they sort of went out on their own. But he wasn't a stern father. My father was very gentle. But he was very, very careful about where his girls were. So we never got very far from home.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that was the attitude that most of the grown-ups had about the girls?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Seems that way. It seemed like most of them stayed at home or close to home anyway. So I think in those days, you know, they weren't very worldly, I guess you'd call it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How about outdoor work? Do you mind if you did outdoor work?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, we didn't have to work outside. No, he never had us work outside. We'd pick potatoes, you know, in potato harvest. But that was the extent of our... I never learned to milk a cow in my life. So I really wasn't that good a farmer's wife. Well, for one reason, there wasn't that much to do. And the neighbors helped each other, so really we didn't have to. When there was haying, the neighbors, the exchange worked, you know. That way we didn't have to do those things. And I don't think he would have let us anyway because he didn't think it was a girl's work. It's so different than the way people think nowadays. I find it very interesting. Well, it was different too. Of course now, you know, the girls drive trucks and they drive tractors. Not that too many worked out, I don't think, only just in harvest. But it's a different, certainly a different generation. Why do you...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know why they felt that way about girls then? Why they shouldn't do the kind of things that men could do?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, I think the thing of it was that they didn't have that much land. But what the neighbors could help each other and the girls didn't have to go out and work. Now I know of some that lived further out, you know, in a bigger community, let's say. And I know that they had to get out and work in haying and even shop grain and things like that. But not in our community, they didn't. That I remember of it all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he mind you going into town, into Genesee?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, we didn't... when we were old, of course when we got older, you know, so we were 16, 17. Well, then we got to go places. But when we were little, we hardly ever went to town. I remember on Fourth of July, we were going to go to town then. So my father gave us each a nickel, which was big, you know. And we were so tickled, and my younger sister, she was lying on the bed, you know, laughing and talking about going to town and how much fun it was going to be. She put her dick in her mouth and swallowed it. And I remember she cried for an hour. So finally my dad said, well, he'd give her another nickel, but this time she was going to hang on to it. I tell you, it wasn't like handing him a five dollar bill like they do nowadays to go someplace. You know, we sure didn't have much money. But we had a good time, a good life.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did your mother do? What were her tasks and the work that she had to do?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, you can imagine with that many children, my mother was a very good seamstress. So she made all her dresses and carded wool and knitted our stockings. And she didn't do much outdoor work either, only help milk the cows, she did do that. But that was relaxation for her, get out of the house. We would bake all our own bread. Well, you know, of course when I started, after I was married too, I did the churning and bread baking and all that, you know. But we learned all that from home, so it wasn't hard. But they seemed to have time to visit friends. They weren't, I don't think as particular with their houses as they are nowadays, maybe. And yet I can see my mother down on her hands and knees scrubbing those bare floors till they were just white. You know, with a scrub brush.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you say they weren't as particular, you mean maybe they were asking for everything in a certain place or something?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, it was orderly too. I just meant that their houses weren't that nice, that you had to really keep them up like you do nowadays. You know, if you have a real nice house and don't keep it up, it can look terrible. But in those days, everybody, they washed an iron and they did just like we do nowadays, only they did it the hard way. They had to have iron that you had to heat on the stove and all this and that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When did they have time for visiting?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh, they always had time in the afternoon. Take your kids and go to the neighbors and visit. Maybe they'd help each other fix gooseberries or pit cherries or something. They were always working, or they always took their handwork along if they weren't doing something else. Oh no, they couldn't be idle with their fingers. I don't think I ever saw my mother sit down for five minutes without doing something with her hands. Even up to the time she passed away. Always did something. Knitting, crocheting, embroidering, patching. Yeah, they were busy people. That's for sure.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The men in the crew, were they all local people from the farm?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh no, not always. The Trenchins used to come into Genesee for the harvest. Because they paid pretty good money for men in the harvest field. If you needed a man, you'd just go into town and they'd be sitting on a bench there in front of the pool hall or someplace. They would hire them to come out. A lot of them were local people, of course. A great many of them were. But there were a lot of Trenchins too. For sewing sacks, they almost had to know. That was kind of a trade. Because you had to work fast. And of course running a steam engine too, you had to know what you were doing. And also a thrashing machine, what they called a machine man. So they had to be kind of special and they got special wages too. But as far as driving the wagons with the shocks and things, why that was... Most any kid could do that in pitch bundles. So, it was quite a thing when they started with their headers. Of course, then they run the headers and run the grain into that. And then the combines, of course, that was the next step. I was so sorry, I had a picture of our thrashing crew and a picture of us girls standing in the doorway. And whatever became of that, I think I burned it when I left Carxton. I had so much stuff that I couldn't move everything. And I think I just thought, well, that's an old thing. I don't care for that anymore. Now I get my ... for it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wanted to ask you, when they moved the wagon, the cookhouse, did you have a hard time keeping everything in place?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, you had to tie everything down. You had cupboards for the dishes and you just had to wire the cupboard doors shut so they wouldn't fall out. And you couldn't cook or anything while you were moving. You know, like if you wanted to cook a roast so you'd have it for your supper that night, you couldn't do it because you couldn't keep the fire going when you were moving. So, oh yes, we had to pack everything off the tables so it didn't shake off. So that was another added chore we had to do. Men have told me that it was a great time of the year because they all had a chance to socialize while out in the crew. And there was an excitement about that time. You feel that was true. It felt like you'd been too busy to take much pleasure in the conversation, in the company. Well, of course, so often when we would come to a farm, you know, they always visited the cooks and the cookhouse. So we had company quite a bit of the time, you know, just for the afternoon. And a lot of times you would ask the lady to probably come and eat dinner with us or something if her man was working with the crew. So it wasn't lonesome at all.

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: But it's really quite an experience.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I suppose you would have gotten to see quite a few places that way in the course of the season.

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: You see, they'd always start way down on the rim, what they call the rim rock, because crops were much earlier there. So they sort of started down there and then they would follow up until they got up into the valley or whatever. Wherever they wanted them to thrash. Manco wasn't the only one that had a thrashing outfit, but he sure got over an awful lot of ground. And it went on for weeks and weeks. And then, of course, if there was a rain, well then they'd have to stop. And that was always a horrible thing because they'd have to stop and they'd have to feed the horses and everything. So it was kind of tough on the farmer, you know, if there came a rain. And we'd have to feed the men because a lot of them couldn't go home. So it had its drawbacks, but all in all they took it as something they sort of expected.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he have, your uncle, did he arrange with the order of the thrashing well in advance of the time he came?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, they would come to him and see if he could come at a certain time. And usually then, like I say, we'd start way down on the rim, which was way down below Genesee, you know. And just work ourselves up towards the grain ripened. And a lot of times you'd have to go back to the same place again too because the grain wouldn't all be ripe at one time, you know, so you'd have to backtrack again. But that was just part of being a thresherman, I guess.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you think of these, what were people like who came just drifted into the area and out again? Were they a very different kind of people?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, no, they were people, mostly, you know, people, single men that probably sort of followed, something like the migrant workers maybe. Because, you know, the harvest probably would be over with down in the Pomeroy country and around in there and then they'd sort of follow the harvest, you might say. And maybe they'd get in 30, 40 days of harvest work, which paid real well, you know. But they didn't have cars or anything, so how they got from one place to the other, I don't know, but... Probably walked, I don't know. Or maybe hopped a freight train or something. Yeah, could be, because trains came into Genesee at that time too, you know. But they did, they more or less followed the harvest like the migrant workers now in berries and... Well, all the things that they raised nowadays. They don't nowadays because they had their combines, and you know, one man can almost combine a field all by himself. If his wife were to drive the truck, why, they can do the whole harvest themselves. In those days it would take all these men to get your harvesting done, so it just goes to show, you know, what progress there has been in the last 40, 50 years.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where would the harvest start?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, it would depend on, I think, lots of times it started in, oh, probably even the last of July. And then usually it was through August and probably all of September. And it would depend on the weather, you know. If we had rain it would take longer. Because I know the year that my husband and I were married, he was still working with a thrashing outfit. And had to lay off to get married because of rain. So he just quit. He was driving a bundle wagon, I guess, or something. And that was the 10th of October. So it would drag out, way out into October sometime. Late grain, you know. But I think most of the time they were through in September. Not before school started by any means, but that didn't seem to make any difference at that time because they hired everything done anyway. Now they need their kids at home, you know, through harvest. I was going to ask you about the migrant fellas.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you see the same ones come back the next year?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Sometimes they would and sometimes not. But I know often they would be the same ones that would come back and work for my uncle. If they didn't live way off some place, you know. But as a rule, they probably were different people that came in. You know how people are when they're kind of drifters. They just go all over the country. They don't come back to the same place very often. But there was always men to get anyway. It isn't like it is now. You can hardly get a man that will go out on a farm and work, you know. Those days I didn't know anything else. I didn't have as much education as I do now. Not so many different jobs.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did you meet your husband?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, I guess I always knew him, maybe. I don't know. We only lived about five miles apart. I suppose probably at a dance or something. I really can't remember when I first met him. Because the folks knew his folks too. But we didn't socialize because, like I said, at that time they belonged to the upper church and we belonged to the lower one. It was at that time. But by the time we got married, the churches had merged. But he was just a farm boy and my father thought he was alright. He was a farm boy. Oh dear.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Your father liked the farm boys better than the town boys. Oh yeah, he trusted the farm boys.

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: They had kind of funny ideas. In those days about the boys in town. They called them sports. We used to laugh.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they dress differently and act differently than the boys on the farm?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, I suppose so. If you lived in town you really didn't have very much to do. They didn't know how to work on a farm or anything. So he kind of thought they couldn't be very much good if they didn't know how to work on a farm. Oh dear. My husband sure knew how to work on the farm. He worked in the fields from the time he was twelve years old. They had a big family too. They had as many children as high folks did when I was eight. So they all had to work.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And he planned on going right on and being a farmer?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Uh huh. Oh yes. We rented a house, the farm that Fred lived on. His father bought that farm. So we farmed it and we lived there twenty-five years. And then we moved to Troy and bought our own farm after twenty-five years of work. We lived there nine years and then we moved to Clarkson. Until my husband died then I moved back up here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How much land did he rent? And my husband?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: We had 160 acres I guess. And then we bought 160 acres up by Troy but part of that was timber land. But we didn't do anything about the timber. We let people come out there and chop wood and haul it off. They wanted it for nothing. But we didn't. Oh he chopped some for our own use but we didn't use that much wood. By that time we had electricity. Although we didn't have an electric stove while we lived on the farm at Troy. Because we did have wood. So we burned wood in our kitchen stove. And I still say that the kitchen stoves were the best. I mean the wood burning stoves. You could make the best bread in those things. What do you think made him better than the electric... I don't know but maybe it was just an idea. But boy it seemed to me I never could bake bread as good in the electric stove as I did in that wood stove. And I've heard other people say that too. But what they was about it I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When did you move to Troy? About when?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: In 1940. We moved up there. Our oldest daughter, the one that lives here now, she was going to school. She went to university and then she went to normal because she wanted to get to work a little quicker. So she took a course in teaching and then she taught the home school up there at Troy. What they call Miller Trestle. And she stayed home then for two years and taught school up there. Well I want to ask you a little about the church when you were young. Now I don't remember if I ask you if you knew why the reason was that they had two different churches or what people said was the reason they had two churches. Well it was because they belonged to different synods. And their teachings weren't just exactly alike. They were different. Which was just so little difference. But you know in those days they were so strict about their church and everything that neither side would give in until they got a minister that was real broad minded. And he said well there was just no sense in two churches standing side by side. And I think it tells in that book who it was that was the minister at the time of the merger.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How close together were these churches?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Half a mile. Just half a mile apart. In fact the one above was right close to where this John Hagan lives now. I think maybe he, well no he isn't on the church land but it was right close there anyway. And then the other one.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you have any idea what the differences or what some differences might be between the synods?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No but I think if you read that book it will tell you. I can't tell you right off because I can't remember. But I know it wasn't much. So it was just a matter of, I said stubbornness mostly with the older people. And then of course as the younger people grew up then they could see that there was no sense to anything like that. So they finally got together.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did it divide the community some in the early days?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Depending on which church you belong to. Yeah it really did to a certain extent. You really associated with the people that belong to your church rather than mingle with those above. And a lot of people lived above the upper church to come down to our church.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you have any other things? Well this is historical...

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well to a certain extent but I mean it wouldn't be of importance to anybody. Well I don't think so because the facts that are already recorded, that's the kind of history that no person is going to be able to tell you as well as the records. But to get a feeling for how people lived and the social life, the social history is different. And what happened to one person is like what happened to many. Well yeah that's true. But we were just saying that you said people also went from above the church to the upper church. There was a lot of people that belonged to the upper church so we'd go right by our church to go up to theirs. There was a lot of people that lived in Blaine at that time that came down to our church. Although Blaine at that time had a Methodist church and it was a Methodist community. But that's been long gone. In fact I must have been quite young, I must have been probably 15, 16 years old when that church was discontinued.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well you were about that age when the two churches combined, weren't you?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah I was the first one that was confirmed in the new church after they merged.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember how it was they merged? Did they build a new church?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: They built a new church, uh huh. And they sold their old church up there and I think that they must have sold... No they didn't sell the parsonage up there because we had a minister live there way after I was married. There was a minister that came and had a big family and they lived out there in the country and that old square building is still there. You know, windows all knocked out and everything. But that used to be the old parsonage that belonged to the upper church. And then we had a building right back of our church that was the parsonage. And my uncle and aunt that lived up in the timber that had the homestead, they bought that after the churches merged. And they lived there and he was janitor of the church for many years.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well where did they decide to put the new church as compared to where the other two?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well I guess on a kind of cemetery they decided to build it there. And it seemed to be the logical place for distance for people who belonged and sort of more central. But I think it was most anaconda cemetery. Do you think the men would... I'm trying to imagine how you could have a community in two different churches.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'm wondering was religion a topic of real debate among the men?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: I think it was among the elders of the church. And boy in those days they were an elder in the church. Now they just about told you what to do and what not to do. And of course the ministers the same. They had their beliefs you know and they weren't going to budge either. So it was a strange thing. We've often wondered how in the world they could do such a thing as to build two churches that close together and still be Lutheran churches. But that's the way it was.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you were kids did you wonder about that?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well I don't think we did so much until we got older. We just took it for granted you know. But of course they were friendly with some of the people in the other church I'm sure. But they certainly weren't. It wasn't like after they merged and you were just one church.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you were young what role did the church have in your life when you were a youngster?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well just about the same as now. We had our societies and our young people's gatherings and Sunday schools and parochial schools. We always went to parochial school in the summertime. Had about two weeks of that. I don't know. It seemed to me like it wasn't too much different than it is now. Of course everything now is on some bigger scale and so much more organized I guess you'd call it. But they, those pioneers, they did pretty good though. Boy I tell you they helped pay the preacher's salary too. If it wasn't for the lady's aid they wouldn't have had much. Because people didn't have money. And you paid the preacher any way you could with potatoes or meat or eggs. They were glad to get that even.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did the lady's aid work on that?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well we worked you know sewing and making things and then every year they had what they call an auction sale. And they sold their goods you know that was for the public. And they made quite a bit of money but that all went to, almost all of it went to pay the preacher. Because well people just didn't have the money that's all there is to it. And if the organist was paid just probably on holidays when they'd have a special offering. I remember they had the baptismal table right by the organ and you put your cents on there and it was only cents too. It wasn't dollars or anything. So if an organist got $25 a year she was well paid. So now you know what they pay him. So you know it's just the way the times were and they thought nothing of it because they didn't know any different.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were the activities mostly that you did in the church? Was it as a kid did they have a lot of Bible study?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No we didn't have anything like that. We just had our Sunday school and two weeks of parochial school during the summer and that was the extent of our Bible studies.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was the parochial school like?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well it would be like a vacation Bible school they have and all the churches now you know. And we studied our Catechism and Bible history. We got quite a bit out of that of course. But boy when you went to Confirmation in those days you learned every blessed word in that book by heart. And the day of your confirmation you probably were asked 50 questions out of that book and you were supposed to know every one of them. So we were drilled believe you me. But nowadays they don't do it that way at all. They don't even quiz them on Confirmation Day. They have a little quiz I think probably a week before in the evening or something. But they're thorough I mean they take notes and they have to. But we just had to memorize. There was no such thing as taking notes you know and asking you about this and that. You memorize that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it in Norwegian?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: I was. The rest of my family weren't. The rest of the kids were in English. But at that time they didn't have English in the church even. But then after they merged then they had English services all the time. For a while I believe they had Norwegian one Sunday and probably English three Sundays. Because some of those old timers didn't understand English even. They hadn't learned it. So for their sake they had one service a month in the Norwegian language. But it was when they merged that they started using English as a service. That's interesting. So there was many steps to be taken before they got where they are today.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember your confirmation?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh very well. There was just one boy and I. And I know they teased us. They said that it looked just like a wedding. We sat up there in front and I was so embarrassed. It was so silly I think about it now. But that boy is still living too. He lives in California.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were you called on to do then?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh we had to stand up in front of the congregation. And the minister would ask us questions out of our catechism. We had to answer it and I did. I never missed a one. The boy missed one or two questions I believe and that was it. If it had all stayed with me I'd be pretty smart today. But I'm afraid it didn't.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there much social life in the church or was that more in the school?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: The men didn't have any organizations in the church. But the ladies were real active and they had big dinners. We had those Norwegian lutefisk dinners down there. In that little tiny parish hall you'd serve three or four hundred people. They'd just have to stand outside and take their turn to come in and eat. I don't know how we did all those things in those days.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would be the occasion for a lutefisk?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: To make money for the church. When we built the new church there were many things to be bought. They had to do carpets and hardware and just a lot of things. They depended on the ladies to furnish most of that which we did. And that was one way of making money besides our yearly auctions that we had.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was one woman chosen to be the head of the church?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah, they had what they called their president and their vice president and their secretary and treasurer. So they had all those things. It was well organized and of course the young peoples had the same. They had the organization, the Luther League. They met. I think they met just about every two weeks if I remember right. Because that was about all we had to go to in those days.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you have parties at Luther League or would it be strictly religious?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh no, no, no. We played games. Oh yes, we served. We turned serving to the young people. Oh no, it was a real recreation. We had a good time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were they the party games like they play in school? Like a skip to my loo?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah, all that kind of stuff. We had to make a lot of our own fun those days. To get in a car and go to a movie or something like that, you know. I don't think I went to a movie until I was probably 14 years old. I'm sure. We got to go to the circus once a year. But then we just got to see the parade, not the circus. But we thought that was the circus, you know. Because they had such good parades those days. They just paraded all our animals and everything down Main Street and Moscow. So when we went to the circus, we thought we'd seen it when we saw the parade. Which was fine because we probably wouldn't have been satisfied if we'd known any different. Think about all those things now and what the kids get to do and see nowadays. But I really think we were more satisfied than they are now. Because, like I said, we didn't know any different.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did school have much activity, social activity going along with it? Or was most of that around the social activity around the church?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, we had what they called... What in the world do they call that? Something they had in the school.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Are you thinking literary and debate?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah, literary society, I think they called it. Because that wasn't when I was real young. That was after a few years. And they used the schoolhouses then too for a lot of parties. Like, later we had clubs. We had a club in the valley called the Bluebird Club. And we used to put on plays and entertainment in the schoolhouses for our families. And that was fun. It showed what talent we had, you know. We weren't so particular then. Whether we knew our lines so well or anything. But we had a lot of fun. And then they sometimes had dances in the schoolhouses.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it alright for you to dance?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah, oh yes, we danced. Of course, our church didn't believe in it then. Oh my, they danced. That was a terrible thing, but we did anyway. We went to country dances and things. But I always think about those poor teachers that had all those kids and tried to cram in eight grades. In the six hours of work, I tell you, they really had something to do. My sister taught in that schoolhouse down there in Kendrick. I think she had thirty-five pupils in all eight grades. But they seemed to get through. In those days, you had to call the county exam to get through your eighth grade. And even after we moved up to Troy, when my daughter taught there at Troy, she had eighth graders and they had to have the county exam. And they said that her two pupils, and one of them happened to be my youngest daughter too, they had the highest grades of any county kid that had taken the exam. But I think that was the last year that they had that. Then they finally quit. But that was in the country school, not in the town, because they didn't have to take those.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you find the school to be a place where you learned a lot?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah, I think we did. But you had to depend on yourself an awful lot because the teacher couldn't help you too much. But I think that's alright. I think that they do that nowadays too. It's sort of up to you. If you want to learn, well you learn. If you don't, well you just don't. Because even now they have so many pupils that they don't get too much individual attention, I don't think.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was school the same kind of length as it is now as far as being most of the year? Or was it short?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, we had our, I think maybe, it might have been only eight months at the time that I went to school. But after I was married and had children, it was always nine months school. But then of course the families were smaller then and they didn't have so many in the country school. My goodness. I don't know how many Elaine had out there at Troy's. She might have had twenty-five though. But I don't know if there was any more than that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were Genesee winters like when you were young?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Cold. Snowy. My howie, you've waded through the snow. It was, um, winters seemed to be harder then than they are now. Or maybe it was just because we didn't have heated houses and things like they do now. But it was awfully cold. I know we used to wade through the snow to get to school. Of course we didn't have very far to go, we only had three-fourths of a mile, which wasn't far. But it was kind of tough going. But we made it. But I don't know, it seemed like we had four seasons at that time. We don't have that anymore. I remember we had early spring. In February and March they'd be out in the fields. And I think the seasons have changed an awful lot. Now we have two winter and summer. So, but then that, I don't know what causes that I'm sure. But as I remember we had four seasons and they were long falls and the winters weren't so long. But they were cold.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Early spring would begin in February?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Uh huh, I think it would begin to get nice in February. March was real nice. That would be nice, I'd like to have that again. I would too. But like I say, the last few years, I know since I moved to my school it's just been from summer right into winter, or winter to summer.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You said you knew Jake Rosenstein? What was he like?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: He was a little short bald headed fellow. Kind of a red mustache. He was a typical Jew. I remember him real well. His wife was, oh she was just like a little princess, a little doll, you know, dark. I can see her sitting behind that counter measuring out goods. She had kind of a stool she sat on. She was real cute.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you say typical Jew, what do you mean? He had a good business sense?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well yes, and then they talked. Their language was like you hear the Jews. They pretend like they're talking like Jewish people. But they have a different, kind of a different brogue in a way. They did at that time. I mean the old Jews, because the young Jews, you can't tell them from the others. But they were, and they were quite proud people, you know, those Jewish people were. I can see her yet. She was always dressed so pretty. The girls were always dressed so nice. They went through high school in Genesee I think. Oh, that girl. They had three.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you know the girls? You knew the girls?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah, uh huh. And I knew their son too, Max.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were they pretty much like anybody else in the community?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah, they were. Yeah, they were. I wasn't, you know, we lived in the country so I didn't know them well, but I knew who they were through the store. But I didn't go to school with them or anything.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he do much of a business in Genesee?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah, he had a big business there. You bet. I don't know why they left Genesee. Probably. Probably, I think there were some other Jewish people there too, and maybe when they left, they left too, I don't know. But they went to California. Except the son, he stayed in Spokane. He had a business up there. Their son was married to a real good friend of mine. In fact, she was our closest neighbor when we were kids growing up together. She just passed away here just a short time ago. But his family never accepted her. Because she was a Gentile. Which was kind of sad, you know. I'll put that there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you know many of the Indians who lived in the, or part Indians who lived in the country?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, yeah, I knew, yes I did. Oh, not too many, but I knew some. My uncle had a farm down on the rim rock, and it was right amongst the Indians. And we used to go down there and visit him, and some of the people would come. But they were mostly half-hat breeds that we knew. But they were just like anybody else.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did that intermarriage come about because of the allotment of the reservation?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: I thought that they gave land to, a certain amount of land to, each Indian or Indian family. Yes, they did. Well, yes, I suppose so. You know, the girls got as well as the boys. I know of two or three white men that married full-blooded Indians. I went to school with a girl, her father was white and her mother was full-blood. But I suppose probably that's how it come about. Some are more quarter breeds, and they were good-looking people. So long ago some of those that I've even forgotten them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you get shivareed when you got married?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh, you bet. On our 25th anniversary, too. We were shivareed again. We had that up at Troy. Well, they had the party for us down in the valley. But we lived up at Troy at that time. That evening they shivareed us again. Oh yes, you bet. That was the thing to do, you know, in those days. And you had to treat them to whatever you had. Away from a lot of those old customs. That one seems like a nice one to me. Well, it was a lot of fun. Sure.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would the whole community turn out for shivaree? Or would it just be the rowdy young kids?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh no, no. It wouldn't be the married couples. Kids, I don't think the kids really went that much. I think it was mostly the married folks that went.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they have to make a lot of noise under your window?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yes. They bang and they shoot up in the air and they had to carry their tin cans and pound and yell in the hall. Oh dear. But everybody was prepared because they knew it was coming, you know, because they did it to everyone that got married. Until it went out of style, I don't remember.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you supposed to wait a while before letting them in? Was that part of the deal?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, they got to pound it out of their system and then you'd open the door and let them come in. And then they'd either dance or just visit or do something.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was this supposed to be the same day you got married?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Mm-hmm. Yeah. Usually, or if you went away right away. We went away right after we were married and then they shivareed us when we got back. But they'd get you sooner or later. This is part of the fun. Mm-hmm. Did many people plant by the signs down the... My father always planted potatoes by the... I don't know whether it was the dark of the moon or the light of the moon, but it was something. Probably the dark. I suppose so. I've forgotten now. And the corn the same way. He always went for the almanac. He was great to read the world almanac, you know, and kind of went by that a whole lot. Tell you different parts of the country which would be the best time for seeding and so on and so forth. Oh yeah, they... I think they pretty much went by the sign of when they should plant, especially potatoes and corn. I don't remember the other vegetables so much. I don't think that they made any difference. You planted those when the ground was warm, I guess. Were there stories from the old country that your kids used to get told by... Oh yeah. Yeah, my grandmother used to tell us stories from the old country about the Nisse... Nisse, she called them. Little folks. They called them... I don't know if there was any truth to them or not, but she said it was. But I don't think so. They were probably just old stories. Yeah, I think they were just folk stories.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember what the little folks were supposed to be like?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh, they always came out at night, you know, and they'd steal things. And so, oh, I don't remember all the things she told me now. But anyway, I remember it was... They called them the little people or the Nisse. That's what they were called. Or the trolls too, you know. They usually were under bridges. You didn't dare to cross the bridge because the troll might get you. They were just fairy tales. She was Norwegian. She was born in Norway, yeah. My mother was too. Oh yeah, she... I think she kind of believed in her. I remember right. Well, it doesn't surprise me because those were... those kinds of stories were so widely known, I think. Yeah, they really were. But I don't remember anything in particular that... that she told me. Only just what we kids thought was fairy tales, of course.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there proverbs that they taught you?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know what I mean? Like a haste makes waste and a stitch in nine saves time. Those are the old American things.

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah, yeah. No, I don't think so. I really don't think so. There's a... I remember when my grandfather and grandmother died, but I... It was in the... seemed to be in the early 1800s. No, no. No, no, no. I don't mean that. Early 19th. In the first part of the 1900s. Yeah, I think my grandfather died probably in 1901… no..… he must have been older... it must have been later than that because I think I was about... I think I was about eight or nine when he died. I really don't remember, but anyway, I was going to write it down then I didn't... Yeah, 1893. The wet year. The wet year. Yeah. Well, of course, that was the year I was born, so all I remember is what I was told. That nobody saved their crops that year. It was just almost starvation for a lot of people. Because the crops were absolutely gone. It rained and rained and rained and rained and they just didn't save anything. And I don't know how my folks got along that year, but I suppose... I suppose that, you know, in those days they would give you credit at the stores. If they knew you were honest, they would give you credit so you could get necessary groceries. And then hold you over till the next year and then you paid when you sold your crop the next year. So I suppose maybe that's... that's what they did.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Most people were in the same boat, right?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah. Yeah, that was all through the country that year. That the drought... or not the drought, but the wet year. And they didn't save. I think they said that it even wasn't hog feed. It was so badly... well, started to decay, you know, and mold. So the animals wouldn't even need it. I wonder if that caused many people to leave and give up on their place. Well, I think they more or less stuck it through though. There were a few, you see, that could take it, could stand the loss. That had probably had more land and had little money too. And I know my father used to borrow money from Jake Cambridge. There are still some of the Cambridges living out there. And old Jake, he would let you have money. Real low interest. And he helped out a lot of people, but I think he must have had money when he came here because they had a lot of land. And they always called him the banker. But I know he let my father have money many times because he knew he'd paid back when he could. And I think that he got some money from him that year. So then... Tied us over, you know. Probably a lot of people might have depended on the few people that did have some money. I think they must have. And I guess maybe too that... Maybe they got a job someplace. I can't remember whether my father ever went away from home and worked or not. But he might have. Of course I was just a little baby then. I don't remember whether they ever told me or not. And now I wish that I had asked more about my grandparents and my descendants way back. Never thought about it. I know just how it is because it's the same way with me. I don't think you asked. Just don't think about it at the time. And now, you know, I just... Now I have a friend that lives in Clarkson. She's 95 years old. And she was pretty smart. She was a school teacher though. And she said that they moved off the farm. Why she told her mother and father that they should sit down and she took notes. And tell everything that they remembered as far back as they could remember. Which they did. And, you know, she wrote Pioneer History after she was 70 years old. Took her a long time to write it. Probably 10 years. But it's in the archives over at Pullman in a book form.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What's her name?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Miss Taylor. Phoebe Bloom Taylor. And she really... In fact, I have her Pioneer History that she gave me. That's all about her folks. Her family and everything. But it was a lot of things in there about how the pioneers lived and everything. And that is really a pioneer. But then, of course, that's over in the Pullman area again. Colfax. And so on.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how do you think that the people got by, the pioneers lived around Genesee?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: From what you've been told about it. Do you think it was... Well... For one thing, you see, things didn't cost so much, those days. You could buy a yard of calico for nickel. A yard. And it took very little to make clothes for your kids. And food and bread, of course, we never bought bread, but if you did buy it, it was a nickel a loaf. Butter, probably 25 cents a pound. And you didn't get too much, but if you had a little bit to sell, you could get a lot for what you raised, you know. I mean, it would buy a lot. Of course, then, of course, they went through all these tough years again, too. Like in 1932, wasn't it, when they had, you know, a real... I don't know what you call it, a recession or a... Depression. Depression or whatever. But then, we, of course, went down to 31 cents a bushel. Do you think that most people... But they survived those things. You just simply did without and you ate what you raised on the farm, that's all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What kind of food did you have mostly when you were young?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, we had, we raised hogs, we had pork and a lot of potato. My father was a potato farmer. We had a lot of potatoes and we always had milk and cream and butter and fruit and vegetables. And, you know, that's about all you need besides buying flour. And then you could take wheat in and get it ground for flour. Because they had a mill where you could get that done. So, really, you didn't have to buy much more than sugar and coffee and... A few staples like that. But they got along with so little. And like I say, your money bought so much more. So, it just seemed like... I know we never went hungry. Didn't have what we'd like to have a lot of times, but we never were hungry. And I don't think any people that we ever knew were hungry. So, I think it was management with the women on their part and they conserved everything. And you made your own soap and you... Well, you just plain did everything that had to be done and made your own quilts. Carted your own wool to put in them. It was just, like I say, it's such a different way of life that you can't compare it at all with the way people do now. But you know, they're kind of getting back to this old stuff, trying to learn some of those arts again. So, maybe it wasn't such a bad age at that.

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: And like I've always said, we didn't know any difference, so we were happy with what we had. There was a few people that had more than others, but it's a rule down in the valley, it was pretty much the same every place. You get along with what you had.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that by the time you came along, things had already improved a lot from what they'd been earlier?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, I suppose the very first pioneers, I'm sure, had it pretty rough, you know. And yet I don't know whether it could have been much worse than it was when my folks started out either. They really started from nothing, too. Yeah, they really did. Started from scratch, like they say. Managed to get a team of horses and a couple of cows and a couple of pigs, and from then on, you did what you could with them. And I wanted to ask you about when you got married, what it was like then.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you have much to start with?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, we didn't. No. His father gave him a team of horses and some old machinery and stuff, and we got a new stove and two new beds. And what else was there? We got new... some chairs, I guess. And that was it. And then we got some things from his folks that they weren't using at that time, because they were pretty well to do at that time. And then my father gave us two pigs. I can see him yet driving those pigs with a stick from his place right across the fence over to where we lived. And we started out with just practically nothing. But he got to use his father's machinery, you see, so we didn't have to buy a lot of stuff right away. And we didn't have a car until we'd been married. Oh, man, I suppose we'd been married three years before we got a car, and all Model T Ford. So it was a little tough when we got started, too. But then at that time we had a little backing, you see, because his father helped us. But we paid him rent, just like anybody else. We got two-thirds the crop and he got a third. But we had quite a scramble to get our kids through college, too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you start having kids soon?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, our boy, our son was born about 13 months after we were married, and then we didn't have this girl that lives here until five years later. And then seven years later we had our youngest daughter. So we weren't burdened with a lot of little kids, you know, one right after the other. But we tried to give them an education, because that's all we could afford to do. They helped themselves quite a bit. My son and my oldest daughter Elaine here, they had a little band that they played when they went to college. They played for dances and sort of made their spending money.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you have many young married friends then at the same time?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: I was organizing these little clubs and one thing and another for sociability. We had a lot of good times, too. It wasn't all work, you know, no play.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember Smoltz very well?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yes, yeah. Oh my, yes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you know then?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, but I'm wondering what the place was like. Oh, this ice cream, we called it the ice cream parlor. Yeah, Ed Smoltz, he was a jolly red-headed guy. And he was a typical ice cream man, we called him. Oh yeah, that was the only place in town that you could go in and sit down and have ice cream and stuff, you know. They didn't, they were there for years and years and years. In fact, one of their daughters still lives in Genesee. She's married to a Roach, Roach the builder. That's one of the Smoltz girls.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it a big meeting place for the kids in Genesee?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, yeah, it was something like, oh, any place, you know, where they gather now, like,… well, for the young folks, not so much the old folks, but it was sort of the gathering place where they'd sit around, slide on the benches like my father used to say. I always think about that. That was the guys that used to sit in it, Smoltz. They sit there and slide on the benches. It says they don't do anything. Oh dear. That's really funny. Yeah, Genesee isn't much anymore. You know, they used to have quite a town there. They had two, three stores, and hardware store, and drug store, and ice cream parlor, and I think they only had one pool hall at that time in Genesee. And it was really quite a, and they had Herman's, they had that store for I suppose 50 years where they sold furniture and stuff, you know. But now there's just nothing there anymore. I was going to ask you how your family felt about Prohibition.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember when that came in?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They did away with the drinking?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Well, I don't remember too much about that. Yeah, I remember at the time that then the bootleggers came in, you see. I remember that. So they sold bootleg whiskey. But I don't think it affected the valley too much. Not that I remember anyway. I know as far as my family were concerned it didn't. I don't know, it might have. I guess there was a lot of people that bought bootleg whiskey, but my father never did. Yeah, I was imagining that they would have, and a lot of people were really glad to see it come because they thought that it would stop the drinking. Yeah, I think that, oh yes, I think as far as, oh you meant how people felt about it. Oh yeah, I think that they were glad when it came in, but they didn't like the bootleggers. They had plenty of those around. I don't think people thought that was what was going to happen after they put it in. No, I don't think so either. You know, but I guess it's something that followed Purdiner every place after that. It went out, I think that bootleg was just practiced every place. And the valley had its share of it too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know how your mother felt about voting?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Did she feel that she should vote as a... I really don't, I don't remember that my mother ever voted. I don't believe she did. If she did, why, I can't remember it. I don't think those days that they thought very much about, oh surely she must have, but it seems to me like that was always left to the men to do that. I might be mistaken, maybe she did. Well, they didn't have the right to vote until almost 1900, the women. No. I just wondered how, if she ever thought about women's rights and that kind of thing. No, oh I'm sure. She was too busy with her family to think of anything like that. And you know, really in those days they didn't think too much about things like that. I remember we just got a paper from the east, and that's the only paper I remember my father having was a Norwegian paper that was printed in South Dakota. And it came twice a week. Until of course after the Genesee had a printing press and they kept the Genesee news. But I don't remember, I don't think they ever had, that is not when I was little, of course they did in the later years of course. But I remember that, that they had this paper that came from the east, and it was in the Norwegian language. And it had sort of an extra little paper in there that was serial stories in it. And I know my mother used to just wait for that paper to come to see how her story was coming. So that's all I can remember about them having any kind of a paper.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder if that would be a romance or a melodrama?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: No, it was a romance I'm sure. Yeah, it was serial. Because I never read it, I could read Norwegian at that time but I can't even read it anymore.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So are you saying that really that probably people weren't very interested in politics?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah, that's what I mean. I don't think that they even thought too much about it. Because what news we did get came in this eastern paper and that was probably a week late by the time they got it out here. I don't know. I know that we never kept Spokane paper or Lewis and didn't have a paper at that time, I don't think. Probably did, but I know we didn't have it. So I don't think that they... The men talk politics. When they got together they always talked politics. I can remember that. It was their politics.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would they figure?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: I suppose if they had run the country it would be run different at that time too. I'm sure that that was it. But the women never talked politics. Never.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did they talk?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: They talked about their sewing and their baking and their kids. They talked about the way they lived I guess. I'm sure politics was way, way out for them… i don't know… like I say, it's been so long ago that I just... No, I think what you're saying, and I've heard something like that before, that that's the way it was with politics and what women and men... The one thing I didn't ask you about that I was meaning to ask you more about was what you did when you were young along the lines of just for enjoyment when you were a kid. The sorts of things you occupied yourself with when you were just working. Oh. I don't know. Really. Don't know how the time went. I guess we were busy helping our mother. But I don't remember that we ever... We were quite a musical family. We spent quite a bit of time singing. And we got sort of taught ourself I guess on the organ. And then we finally got a piano. The whole family sang. So we did a lot of that, I remember. But...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What kind of songs would they be related to?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh, no, that would be the songs of the day, you know. We had, I guess we had phonographs. We'd get songs that way or hear them, you know, how you'd dance as they'd play some of the new songs that were new at that time. And I don't know. Of course we had a choir in our church. We always sang in the choir. But as far as, you know, because we just didn't... We didn't get around to do anything, go anyplace or do anything much. Only just right in the neighborhood.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did girls have dolls that played house when you were young? Like they did when I was young?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: I think that the only dolls that I remember... I didn't get a china doll until I was 15 years old. Otherwise we just had rag dolls. And we used to play house just like kids do nowadays, but we didn't have anything to play with. We made our own little tables, you know. Broken glass would be our dishes. And I remember when the neighbor kids would come and my father had a nice horse one time that died and we all felt so bad. So we had a funeral for this horse. And we sang and we brought flowers and put on the grave and all such stuff as that. Stuff that you had to think about yourself, you know. I don't think kids do anything like that nowadays. That sounds like you had to use your imagination. Yeah, we had to use our imagination for anything that we did. Games or anything. We didn't have any games or anything to play with.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there a lot of made up games that you played?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah, we'd make up games between ourselves. And of course we were great on going to the neighbors and playing, you know. But we always had to take the little kids along so that mother could have a little free time to do what she was doing. So it was... I never remember of any time that I really got to go someplace and play unless some of the younger kids had to tag along. And we had to look after them. But then that was just something that we knew we had to do, so that was alright. Never even thought about going without having to drag the kids along.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was her day laid out from beginning to end pretty much what she'd have to do?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah, yes indeed. You had this day for baking and that day for churning and washing and ironing. Because, you know, you'd have to with a big family like that. Otherwise you'd just be in a muddle. Yeah. And I think that stayed with me too because when I went to housekeeping, I did the very same thing. I had a Monday for washing, Tuesday for ironing, Wednesday to bake bread and churn and Thursday so and so. And on down the line. And I know on Saturday we always had to... Mother would always lay out all our clothes for Sunday school in the morning so that everybody knew where their clothes were. Oh you bet, it had to be a system to it or... They couldn't have done it. And I think most of the women were the same way. They had their schedule pretty well planned out. But they only went to town probably once every two weeks or so to buy groceries.

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: So it was an entirely different way. I imagine from what you're saying that on a day, on a given day, she probably wouldn't have much time to just sit around either. Oh no, I don't ever remember. And if she did, like I say, her hands were busy. Either at the sewing machine or crocheting or knitting. And she did that after she moved to town and she didn't have so much to do. She still kept busy with her hands and I'm pretty much the same way only now. My hands aren't working that good. After I broke them, why they're pretty stiff and achy. I'm starting in a little bit though. I'm starting in African again now. Oh that's good. So I hope I'll be able to do.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Will this be the first thing that you have made since you had the accident?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: The first thing with the needle. But my hobby is making these dolls. Over there on the table, those granny dolls. And I have made those since I've been back again. I've got to keep busy at some things. I'd like to be out helping a little bit in the yard. The thistles get away from my daughter. They're just so thick up here on the hill, you know. But I can't do anything yet. I'm scared to death of the gypsies. I know one time we went to parochial school. And there was a bunch of gypsies came and we, our folks had told us that they might steal kids. And I tell you, we ran until we were so out of breath. So finally we couldn't run any further so we crawled under the fence and hid in a field. Because we were so scared they were going to steal us. But even after I was married the gypsies would go through with their wagons. And they would always stop and want to sell you a lace or trade for food or something. I remember one time I was just through baking bread and they'd always have some story about their grandmother was sick and needed something special, you know, and a fruit. If I could just give them a jar of fruit or a glass of jelly for their grandmother, well that wasn't so at all. That was just their tale, you know. So one time I had just baked bread and I had probably six, seven loaves of bread there. So they wanted to know if they couldn't trade me some lace for bread. So I said, oh sure, I'll trade them. So they traded me some lace. I don't know how many yards of lace I got for three loaves of bread. But it was grandmother then too that was so hungry. But then after a couple years, that was the end of that, I think they weren't allowed to stop in the towns anymore. And they don't travel through anymore. But they did, they went through every year.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think they stole as much as people said?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Oh yeah, absolutely. They'd get into the stores, you know, and they had hundreds of pockets, you know, in their clothes. And they would steal all right. But I watched them pretty close. They'd come to my house, you know. In fact, I didn't let them in. I let one lady in at one time because she was going to get bread then for this lace. But the rest of them I wouldn't let them in. Because they'd just wander all through your house and everything, you know, if you didn't watch them. But that's a thing of a past too. That was in 1917, I guess. The last time they went through.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you hear about the IWWs much at all?

speaker: Palma Hanson Hove
words: Yeah, yeah, I remember. And of course at that time too, they brought all these boys out from New York, you know. And they planted all these groves and things around here. Because that was supposed to be the IWWs that they found work for. But they had a real camp down there by Genesee and they planted a lot of trees for people. And some of the boys married some of the local girls and stayed out west. Yeah, they had a lot of those all right. Well, I think that was at the time too, where it was kind of a recession then too. And they didn't know what to do with all these people, you know, in towns. They were starving and everything. Was that during the Roosevelt administration? Yeah, he set up those camps. CC camps, they called them.
